newsitem.title: INDIA: India set to celebrate freedom at midnight.
newsitem.headline: India set to celebrate freedom at midnight.

text.p: India commemorates a half century of independence on Thursday, rejoicing over freedom from British rule but saddened by the nation's unfulfilled legacy.
An evening parade of thousands of citizens through the capital and a special midnight session of parliament were to mark the 50th anniversary of India's "tryst with destiny".

At the stroke of midnight on August 14-15, 1947, more than two centuries of British colonial rule over the vast subcontinent came to an end. In the words of the first prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru, India awoke to life and freedom.
"A moment comes which comes but rarely in history, when we step out of from the old to the new, when an age ends, and when the soul of a nation long suppressed finds utterance," he said.
India's current rulers were to gather at midnight in the same parliament hall where Nehru spoke.
There they will listen to recordings of his words and those of the nation's spiritual father, Mahatma Gandhi, who was gunned down five months after his dream of independence was realised.

From the start, India's independence was tinged with sadness as the stark division of the subcontinent into two nations -- India and Pakistan -- was accompanied by the massacre of hundreds of thousands and the uprooting of millions of families.
Freedom at midnight in August 1947 was followed two months later by war with Pakistan over Kashmir. Three months after that, Gandhi was shot dead by a Hindu fanatic.
This year's celebrations, too, have been bitter-sweet.
"The legacy of the greatest mass movement of the 20th century has been squandered," Outlook magazine said. "The soaring hope and joy of 1947 is today tempered with cynicism and despair."
"India has got over its traumatic birth pains," India Today magazine editor Aroon Purie wrote. "But celebration is tinged with sadness, if not downright anger."

Countless newspaper articles and television programmes listed the many accomplishments of the world's most populous democracy: virtual self-sufficiency in agriculture, a space programme, a record of peaceful transfers of power.

But they also drew attention to the long list of corruption cases against politicians, militancy in Kashmir and the northeast, continued tension with Pakistan and poverty afflicting more than one third of the country's 960 million people.

A poll in India Today showed that 88 percent of India's citizens would like to be reborn Indian, but only 29 percent said they are better off today than five years ago. One in three predicted India would split into separate states within 50 years.
The front pages of Thursday's newspapers were dominated by two events that highlighted continuing contradictions.

In one case, parliamentarians all but got into a brawl over the arrest of a leading politician in a corruption case in Bihar state. In the other, an activist Supreme Court ordered employers to prevent sexual harassment in the workplace.

Among the many speeches will be one in parliament by President Kocheril Raman Narayanan immediately after midnight. Narayanan, who was elected to the largely ceremonial post last month, is India's first low-caste president.

On Friday morning (0130 GMT), Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral will make a nationally televised address from the ramparts of Delhi's 17th century Red Fort. Gujral and his Hindu family fled from Lahore to Delhi after partition drew a blood-stained border through their home region of Punjab.
